units.passage: You are welcome to use generative AI tools (such as ChatGPT, Google Gemini, Microsoft Copilot, Claude, etc.) in this class as doing so aligns with the course objectives
units.policy: Students are welcome to use generative AI tools in this class as doing so aligns with the course objectives of Creating Mission and Vision Statements, Creating a Sample Budget, and Creating Plans for their own Performing Arts Organization or Museum.
units.why: "You are welcome to use generative AI tools ... in this class as doing so aligns with the course objectives of Creating Mission and Vision Statements, Creating a Sample Budget, and Creating Plans" permits AI for the named assignments only, a per-assignment rule (P04), may; the sentence itself permits use.

units.passage: Formulate general guiding principles concerning GAI use at Cal Poly, in consultation with colleges and divisions and other stakeholder communities, which should determine specific policies appropriate to their needs (see, e.g., Ohio CTLT (2025, September), “Developing a University-wide Position Statement on GenAI in Teaching and Learning”).
units.why: The principles "should determine specific policies appropriate to their needs" in colleges and divisions, delegating specifics (P04).

units.passage: In instructional settings, this means the Instructor of Record has broad latitude to determine whether and how generative AI may be used, provided this use is consistent with applicable policies and rules governing data security and instruction at UCR. 5.
units.why: Principle 4 gives "the Instructor of Record ... broad latitude to determine whether and how generative AI may be used", so the rule is set per instructor, P04.

units.passage: Consider how students can utilize generative AI, consistent with your course standards.
units.why: "Consider how students can utilize generative AI, consistent with your course standards" leaves student uses to the instructor's course standards, P04.

units.passage: As of Summer 2025 neither UCSB nor the UC system has a formal policy on generative AI in teaching and learning contexts.
units.why: The page states "neither UCSB nor the UC system has a formal policy on generative AI in teaching and learning contexts". This leaves the decision to instructors, P04.
units.fit_note: Says no formal institutional policy exists; the delegation to instructors is implied by the surrounding advice.

units.passage: If you’re not sure how to start creating an AI policy, consider what you would do if the following scenarios occurred in your course. Then look at the policy examples linked after the scenarios. (Note that only some of these scenarios will be relevant to each course.)
units.why: Instructors who are unsure how to begin are told to consider "what you would do if the following scenarios occurred" (translation, summarizing, quiz practice, a student-built tutor bot, coding and debugging, unequal paid access). This prompts each instructor to decide per scenario, P04.

units.passage: We recommend that you design an generative AI policy that aligns with the specific ethics and practices of your discipline, your department, and your course.
units.why: "We recommend that you design an generative AI policy that aligns with the specific ethics and practices of your discipline, your department, and your course" recommends tailoring policy to context; the decision rests with each instructor (P04).

units.passage: If you do choose to incorporate the sample language, edit it in accordance with your expectations for your course.
units.why: "edit it in accordance with your expectations for your course" tells instructors to adapt the sample language, leaving wording and stance to each course (P04).
units.fit_note: Specifically instructs adapting provided template text.

units.passage: Your message to students about the use of generative AI (and academic integrity in general) should reflect your teaching philosophy, the priorities of your department, and the conventions of your field.
units.why: "should reflect your teaching philosophy, the priorities of your department, and the conventions of your field" says policy messaging follows local context and is left to the instructor (P04).

units.passage: What are your personal and professional stances on AI use? Why?
units.why: The prompt "What are your personal and professional stances on AI use? Why?" asks the instructor to settle and justify their own position as a component of their course policy, so the rule is left to the instructor (P04), not an instruction to explain rules to students.
units.fit_note: A: Asks for the instructor to explain their stance, which also touches P66. B: Asks instructors to articulate their stance and reasons as a required component.

units.passage: For which of the following types of tasks will AI use be allowed or disallowed?
units.why: "For which of the following types of tasks will AI use be allowed or disallowed?" asks instructors to sort tasks (brainstorming, writing code, debugging, tutoring) into allowed and disallowed, so the rule is set per activity (P04).
units.fit_note: A checklist of task categories to rule on, not named tiers.

units.passage: Which specific AI tools will be allowed or disallowed, and under what conditions?
units.why: "Which specific AI tools will be allowed or disallowed, and under what conditions?" asks instructors to name tools (ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, Grammarly) and conditions, a per-instructor decision (P04).
units.fit_note: Asks instructors to name tools, including embedded predictive text and Grammarly; no rule is set.

units.passage: Each course may have its own rules and expectations regarding AI usage, set by the instructor.
units.why: "Each course may have its own rules ... set by the instructor" delegates AI rules to instructors; P04 chosen over P11 because the focus is who sets the rule.

units.passage: Students should carefully read the syllabus and course materials to understand these guidelines
units.why: 'Students should carefully read the syllabus and course materials to understand these guidelines' follows 'Each course may have its own rules ... set by the instructor'; it is the student side of instructor-set rules. The same duty ('Students are responsible for understanding and following the guidelines provided in each course syllabus') was coded P04 by both coders in the terms document, so P04

units.passage: Expectations for the use of Generative AI may differ between courses and instructors.
units.why: "Expectations ... may differ between courses and instructors. Students are responsible for understanding and following the guidelines provided in each course syllabus", leaving rules to instructors, P04.

units.passage: Students are responsible for understanding and following the guidelines provided in each course syllabus, assignment description, or related communication.
units.why: "Students are responsible for understanding and following the guidelines provided in each course syllabus, assignment description" is a student duty to follow course rules; P11 scoped to each course, but the duty to follow fits P29-style ownership less, so P04.

units.passage: Students should be aware that faculty make the ﬁnal decisions regarding the use of AI in their courses.
units.why: "faculty make the ﬁnal decisions regarding the use of AI in their courses" assigns the decision to faculty, P04.
